extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in mathematical research news (mathematicians and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: A short news/blog post announcing and commenting on new preprints and published papers that claim to complete/clarify a major mathematical proof (here: Poincaré/Geometrization). Emphasizes sources, level of detail, publication/refereeing status, and implications for recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail in the proof / worked-out details
rubrics_metrics.description: Morgan and Tian give a complete proof of the Poincaré conjecture; other sources for worked out details of Perelman’s argument are the notes by Kleiner and Lott, and the recent paper by Cao–Zhu. Cao–Zhu provide fewer details than Morgan–Tian, but do give a proof of geometrization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the amount of detail supplied matters: some accounts supply more worked-out steps than others. When evaluating a paper claiming to carry out Perelman's program, compare how thoroughly it fills in Perelman’s arguments and where it supplies or omits detailed derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing / reputable publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: This paper is in the process of being refereed and should ultimately appear as a book in the monograph series that the Clay Math Institute publishes with the AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that peer review and publication in established venues (refereed journals or reputable monograph series) are important markers for the mathematical community’s acceptance of the result. Note the contrast with papers initially available only in paper-only journal issues or behind paywalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope / clarity about what is proven
rubrics_metrics.description: Morgan and Tian just provide a proof of Poincaré, not the full geometrization conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims, distinguish precisely what theorem is being proved (e.g., Poincaré vs. full geometrization). Clear statements of scope prevent conflation of partial results with complete solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness as the central criterion for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Perelman put it: 'If the proof is correct, then no other recognitions are necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects a normative stance that the primary evaluative standard is mathematical correctness; recognition (prizes, honors) should follow from verified correctness rather than publicity or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community validation affects honors/recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Latest rumor ... the Fields Medal committee has definitely chosen Perelman as a Fields medalist, with the appearance of these detailed proofs using his arguments clinching the deal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that formal honors often depend on the community having accessible, validated accounts (detailed proofs) that corroborate the original claim; publicized, detailed expositions can influence committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accessible expositions for non-experts
rubrics_metrics.description: What is needed is a very simplified description of how Poincaré’s Conjecture was solved by Perelman. All the articles that have appeared so far, including several in the NYT, do not quite get it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating major mathematical breakthroughs to the broader public, produce simplified, accurate expositions that convey the core ideas without misleading or over-sensationalizing; lack of clear exposition can leave the public confused about contributions and significance.
